issues.label: Motion to introduce new evidence on appeal
Interpretation of the Seabird Order in Council language
Contextual interpretation of the Order including provincial legislation
Conclusion on whether the entire aboriginal interest was extinguished
Reversion of land to the Band if interest extinguished

result.overall: The Federal Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding that the Seabird Order in Council did not clearly and plainly extinguish the entire aboriginal interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor, so the land remains "in the reserve" for taxation purposes under s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act.

themes.name: Interpretation of Aboriginal Interest Extinguishment
themes.summary: The Court analyzed whether the Seabird Order in Council clearly and plainly extinguished the entire aboriginal interest in the land, applying principles from the Supreme Court's Osoyoos decision.

themes.name: Contextual Interpretation of Order in Council
themes.summary: The Court considered the provincial legislation, prior easements, and agreements to interpret the Order in Council and the extent of the interest transferred.

themes.name: Motion to Introduce New Evidence on Appeal
themes.summary: The Court allowed the appellant's motion to introduce new evidence about the highway resting on leased lands, which could affect the legal analysis of the interest transferred.

themes.name: Legal Framework and Fiduciary Duty
themes.summary: The Court applied the fiduciary duty of the Crown and the principle that ambiguities in extinguishment of aboriginal interests must be resolved in favour of the Band.

arguments.quote: the respondent appealed the assessments to the Seabird Island Indian Band Board of Review ... arguing that the cable system was not on land, "in the reserve" within the meaning of s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act
arguments.claim: The respondent argued the cable system was not on land "in the reserve" and thus not taxable by the Band.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the land remains in the reserve, so the argument failed.

arguments.quote: the Board held that the land and the cable system were "in the reserve" and, therefore, were properly assessed by the appellant
arguments.claim: The Board found the land and cable system were in the reserve and taxable by the Band.

arguments.quote: the Appeal Judge ... allowed the appeal, holding that the property was not "in the reserve" and, therefore, it was not taxable by the Band
arguments.claim: The Federal Court Trial Division allowed the appeal, holding the land was not in the reserve and not taxable by the Band.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court overturned this decision based on Osoyoos principles.

arguments.quote: the appellant made a motion to introduce new factual evidence ... that a part of the Lougheed Highway rests on lands that are not owned by the province absolutely, but instead are leased
arguments.claim: The appellant sought to introduce new evidence that part of the highway rests on leased lands, challenging the necessity of fee simple ownership.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court allowed the motion, finding the evidence credible and potentially outcome-affecting.
arguments.gap: The evidence was not available at trial and could not have been discovered earlier.

arguments.quote: the respondent relies heavily on the language of the provisions of the Highway Act ... which it emphasizes is quite different than the language of the provincial statute in Osoyoos
arguments.claim: The respondent argued the Highway Act's language shows the province intended to acquire fee simple ownership, unlike in Osoyoos.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court held the provincial legislation is contextual but not determinative of federal intention.

arguments.quote: the respondent argues that such an absolute extinguishment was necessary for constitutional reasons ... the province would be unable to build and maintain the Lougheed Highway
arguments.claim: The respondent argued constitutional necessity required complete extinguishment of aboriginal interest for provincial laws to apply.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found s. 88 of the Indian Act allows provincial laws to apply unless inconsistent, rejecting this argument.

arguments.quote: the respondent argues that, had the federal government intended to grant to the province less than an absolute interest in the land, it would have used language similar to that in Order in Council P.C. 1953-30
arguments.claim: The respondent argued the different language in the 1953 Order shows the federal government intended a different, lesser interest in that case, implying full extinguishment here.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found this reasoning unpersuasive and the 1953 Order not determinative.
arguments.quote_snapped: The respondents argue that, had the federal government intended to grant to the province less than an absolute interest in the land, it would have used language similar to that in Order in Council P.C.

arguments.quote: the 1961 agreement ... acknowledges that the permission of the federal government was necessary to erect power lines on Reserve land
arguments.claim: The appellant argued the 1961 agreement shows the Band's interest in the land was recognized, supporting that the land remains in the reserve.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court found the agreement ambiguous and a neutral factor.
arguments.quote_snapped: and one or more lines of wire for the distribution of electrical energy and for communication and television purposes." All parties to that agreement expressly realized that permission was necessary because the land was "Reserve land within the meaning of the Indian Act", as it read at the time.

holdings.quote: it cannot stand in the light of the Supreme Court's decision
holdings.statement: The Federal Court Trial Division decision is overturned as inconsistent with the Supreme Court's Osoyoos decision.
holdings.quote_snapped: 82, can stand in the light of the Supreme Court's decision.

holdings.quote: the appellants motion to adduce this evidence is granted, with costs in the cause
holdings.statement: The Court allowed the motion to introduce new evidence on appeal.

holdings.quote: the interpretation that impairs the Indian interests as little as possible should be preferred, so long as the ambiguity is a genuine one
holdings.statement: Ambiguities in extinguishment of aboriginal interests must be resolved in favour of the Band, preferring minimal impairment.

holdings.quote: because of the genuine ambiguity in the Seabird Order, it must be interpreted to mean that the entire aboriginal interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not extinguished
holdings.statement: The Seabird Order did not clearly and plainly extinguish the entire aboriginal interest in the corridor.

holdings.quote: land remains in the reserve for the purposes of s. 83(1)(a)
holdings.statement: The land remains "in the reserve" for taxation purposes under s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act.

holdings.quote: the Appeal Judge's decision cannot stand in light of Osoyoos, supra
holdings.statement: The Appeal Judge's decision is set aside because it conflicts with the Osoyoos principles.

holdings.quote: the Band is entitled to exercise the powers granted by s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act
holdings.statement: The Band may assess and tax the respondent's cable system under s. 83(1)(a).

holdings.quote: the appellant acknowledges that it is not entitled to tax the province in respect of land in the corridor
holdings.statement: The Band's taxation powers do not extend to the province itself, only to private interests like the respondent.

holdings.quote: even under the Indian Act, the Band does not have an unfettered right to enact by-laws that are incompatible with the interest created pursuant to s. 35
holdings.statement: The Band's by-laws must be compatible with the interests granted to the province under s. 35.

holdings.quote: Because, for purpose of s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act, the Band's entire interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not removed from the Reserve, it is unnecessary for me to consider whether the land would revert back to the Band
holdings.statement: The Court declined to decide the issue of reversion of land to the Band if the interest had been extinguished.

holdings.quote: This appeal should be allowed, the decision of the Appeal Judge should be set aside and the appeal from the Seabird Island Indian Band Board Review should be dismissed with costs to the appellant
holdings.statement: The appeal is allowed, the Appeal Judge's decision set aside, and the Board's decision reinstated with costs to the appellant.

rebuttals.quote: the Appeal Judge was not convinced that anything less than fee simple title would enable a province to build and maintain a highway
rebuttals.point: The Appeal Judge found fee simple ownership necessary to build and maintain the highway
rebuttals.court_answer: The Court found no evidence supporting this and admitted new evidence showing leased land suffices, rejecting the necessity of fee simple.

rebuttals.quote: the respondent argues that such an absolute extinguishment was necessary for constitutional reasons
rebuttals.point: The respondent argued constitutional necessity required complete extinguishment
rebuttals.court_answer: The Court rejected this, citing s. 88 of the Indian Act allowing provincial laws to apply unless inconsistent.

rebuttals.quote: the respondent relies heavily on the language of the provisions of the Highway Act
rebuttals.point: The respondent argued the Highway Act's language shows the province intended fee simple ownership
rebuttals.court_answer: The Court held the provincial legislation is contextual but not determinative of federal intention, which must be clear and plain.

authorities.quote: Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver (Town), [2001] S.C.J. No. 82
authorities.why: The Court applied the interpretive principles and fiduciary duty outlined in Osoyoos to the Seabird Order.

authorities.quote: Opetchesaht Indian Band v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 119
authorities.why: Cited for the requirement of clear and plain intention to extinguish aboriginal interests.

authorities.quote: Canadian National Railway Co. v. Matsqui Indian Band (1998), 162 D.L.R. (4th) 649
authorities.why: Cited for the principle that clear and plain intention is required to extinguish aboriginal interests.

authorities.quote: Amchem Products Inc. v. British Columbia (Workers' Compensation Bd.), [1992] S.C.J. No. 110
authorities.why: Cited for the test to admit new evidence on appeal.

authorities.quote: Glaxo Wellcome PLC v. Canada (Minister of National Revenue - M.N.R.), [1998] F.C.J. No. 358
authorities.why: Cited for the Court's discretion to admit new evidence to avoid undue burden and ensure a complete record.

left_open.quote: Because, for purpose of s. 83(1)(a) of the Indian Act, the Band's entire interest in the Lougheed Highway corridor was not removed from the Reserve, it is unnecessary for me to consider whether the land would revert back to the Band
left_open.issue: Reversion of land to the Band if interest extinguished
left_open.reason: The Court found it unnecessary to decide this issue given its conclusion on extinguishment.
